newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - March 5.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - March 5.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories Wednesday:

* CNA Financial announced the resignations of the president of its life insurance unit and the unit's chief administration officer following complaints by two female employees about offensive remarks.

* With negotiations between Conrail, CSX and Norfolk Southern on an equitable division of Conrail, rail experts think the creation of a transcontinental railroad may be the next step in the mergers that have swept the rail industry since deregulation in 1980.
* The downgrade of earnings expectations for AT&T is raising questions about the overall earnings outlook for the stock market, where the Dow industrials have lost nearly 215 points in two weeks.

* Just a few months ago Uzbekistan was the darling of Western investors, but today there is little evidence of the short-lived boom. The International Monetary Fund has suspended the republic's $180 million loan program, and many executives from small- and medium-sized Western businesses are freezing their investments or pulling out.
* Sales of new homes rose 8.6 percent in January, and the Conference Board said its index of leading indicators climbed three-tenths of one percent in January, the biggest advance since May.
* The yield on the 30-year bond rose to 6.86 percent from 6.83. The dollar touched a three-year high of 1.7152 German marks before settling at 1.7146.

* Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan denied that he was trying to talk the markets down last week by warning that investors might be unduly optimistic. Greenspan, who testified before the House Budget Committee, also urged the appointment of a commission to provide a better estimate of inflation.
* A plan to cut jobs by French carmaker Renault SA shows how the European push toward unity can collide with the tradition of the social safety net.
* Ford Motor said U.S. sales fell 3.2 percent in February.
* Dayton Hudson reported fourth quarter earnings of $1.27 per share before charges, and Federated Department Stores reported higher operating earnings of $1.39 per share.
* The Financial Accounting Standards Board will change the way earnings per share are calculated, and as a result the diluted earnings per share figure will carry more significance.
* The creditors' committee of Barney's rejected a $240 million bid from Dickson Concepts International Ltd.
* Analysts seem to like the stocks of scrap metal recyclers and of service companies that turn steel into usable parts, but Wall Street is divided on old-line manufacturers like USX.
* Warning labels on consumer products have become increasingly elaborate and embarrassingly obvious as product makers seek to avoid costly personal-injury lawsuits.
* Besides responding to flagging sales with discounts on its sandwiches, McDonald's will also begin a promotion based on the board game called Monopoly.
* Sony plans to introduce a line of television studio equipment that can produce digital, high definition programming.
